items.title: Poisoning the corpora of protein design systems during pre-training and retrieval
items.abstract: Protein foundation models increasingly support the generation of novel biological sequences, yet their reliance on large public datasets creates opportunities for adversarial manipulation of the material they learn from and retrieve. We investigate two data-only poisoning attacks against protein design systems, targeting the pre-training corpus of autoregressive protein language models and the retrieval corpus of a text-guided protein generator. For the first, we pre-trained ProtGPT2 and ProGen2 variants of 300 million parameters, introducing poisoned protein sequences containing one of two triggers followed by one of three payloads. Across all poisoned runs, both architectures acquired highly reliable trigger-dependent generation under uniform and ramped poisoning schedules. Under ramped exposure, the earliest majority activation occurred after only 200 contaminated examples, while for the uniform schedule earliest activation occurred around 5000 poisoned samples. For the second attack, we inserted records into a retrieval corpus system without modifying its weights or decoding procedure. A single query-aware record captured a top-16 retrieval position for 58\% of templated requests and 97\% of free-text requests. Conditional on successful poisoned retrieval, 62\% of requests produced altered sequences, while 19-21% acquired the inserted domain by profile-HMM homology. A universal query-unaware attack using 1,500 records also achieved substantial retrieval capture and domain transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that adversarial protein sequence contributions can establish persistent, sequence-specific behaviour during pre-training or redirect protein generation at inference, while leaving ordinary model behaviour largely preserved. Our work establishes the integrity and biological provenance of protein sequence data as critical safeguards for generative protein design systems.

items.title: Polling Without People: Can Silicon Samples of CASM-Inspired LLM Personae Mimic Human Respondents in Pre-Election Polling?
items.abstract: We introduce a framework for simulating pre-election survey responses with large language model (LLM) synthetic personae.Drawing on the Cognitive Aspects of Survey Methodology (CASM) literature, our approach combines synthetic biographies, salient-event memories and conditional news exposure with a staged cognitive process for answering turnout and candidate-choice questions.We apply the framework to a single weekly wave for the 2026 US House elections and produce national and district estimates using multilevel regression and post-stratification.Relative to a demographicsonly synthetic personae baseline, CASM-inspired enrichment shifts estimates towards Democrats, consistent with the direction suggested by contemporary polling.However, the estimated Democratic margin is 18.7 percentage points, compared with 8.7 points in the polling average.Personae randomly assigned to news-based judgement construction produce a larger Democratic margin than retrievers, who are not exposed to news, although uncertainty is substantial.These comparisons show that our enrichment strategy changes synthetic responses in the correct direction, but do not isolate the effects of all components or establish predictive accuracy conclusively.The framework offers a structured approach to studying synthetic survey responses whilst highlighting persistent challenges of leftward bias, uncertainty calibration and benchmarking novel methodologies during an election campaign.

items.title: Polymer-Linked Nanoparticle Networks Running on Heat Can Act as Computing Devices
items.abstract: Abstract Developing physical neural network (PNN) hardwares is important to next-generation artificial intelligence systems. Phononic devices─using heat current to encode and process information─is one of the solutions to neuromorphic computing. In this work, we backmap an artificial neural network (ANN) into a PNN simulation model using polymer networked nanoparticles (PNNPs). Our atomistic simulation results demonstrate that the polymer-linked nanoparticle networks can potentially realize information processing─viz., classification of input temperatures according to the output heat currents. Using high-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the trust region Bayesian optimization (TuRBO) methods, we tune the plasticity of polymer linkers and the temperatures of nanoparticles─28 parameters in total─to optimize the performance of the PNNP machines, which is analogous to tuning of the weights and bias of the corresponding ANNs. After five rounds of high-throughput MD simulations, we demonstrate that the PNNP machine can better label different input temperatures, and thus its performance is improved. We also use a testing data set to verify the heat flow outputs from the top five PNNP machines in each round.

items.title: Positioning AI as a Tool to Revitalise Kenya's Higher Education Sector
items.abstract: The Kenyan education system is undergoing reform through the Competency-Based Education (CBE) and through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI). In the higher education sector, both educators and students are embracing AI as a powerful tool in the learning process. Students, many of whom are more techno-savvy than their teachers, have embraced AI excitedly. This chapter employed a qualitative methodology to analyse selected AI policies applied in Kenya to interrogate how the adoption of the technology is harnessed in the higher education sector. Findings indicate that some of the selected AI policies do not adequately address Kenya's higher education issues. The study further established that a huge segment of the higher education sector has not yet institutionalised AI adoption into policy. The chapter argues that Kenya's higher education sector must actively participate in the AI policy and regulation discussion to ensure that the innovation is embraced in the ongoing education reforms.

items.title: Possibility of Aporia as Experience in LLM Interaction
items.abstract: This study examines the possibility of aporia within human-LLM interactions, proposing the concept of "non-dialogic aporia" to describe an ontological and relational impasse where a user projects reciprocity onto a syntactic system lacking semantic understanding. Grounded in classical philosophy, the analysis integrates John Searle’s distinction between syntax and semantics, Martin Buber’s relational framework, Martin Heidegger’s critique of technology as a standing-reserve (Bestand), Jacques Derrida’s theory of the trace and difference, Luciano Floridi's concept of the "Inforg" and David J. Gunkel's machine ethics. Using the withdrawal of the GPT-4o model as a case study, the essay demonstrates that while LLMs remain non-conscious computational resources, human users can experience profound mourning and ethical interpellation. Ultimately, non-dialogic aporia highlights not the personhood of the algorithm, but the tendency of the hybrid human subject to confront its own reflection and externalized mental habitat within the infosphere.

items.title: Post-Purchase Emotional Collapse: LLM-Assisted Analysis of Online Consumer Complaint Narratives
items.abstract: Online shopping environments involve interactions shaped by trust, responsiveness, speed, and personalization. When post-purchase service failures occur, customer reactions may extend beyond dissatisfaction to cumulative emotional disruption, including regret, frustration, exhaustion, perceived betrayal, and trust erosion. Despite extensive research on service failure and complaint behavior, limited attention has been given to progressive emotional breakdowns across digital consumption journeys. Addressing this gap, the study introduces post-purchase emotional collapse (PPEC), defined as a cumulative emotional breakdown resulting from repeated service failures and unresolved negative experiences across customer touchpoints. Using a qualitative content analysis design, the study analyzes 1,000 consumer complaints from sikayetvar.com via Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted emotional coding, touchpoint identification, metaphor analysis, and narrative classification, with human validation on a subsample. Findings suggest delivery failures as the most frequently coded rupture point, with anger, disappointment, and regret as the most frequently coded primary emotions. Complaint narratives include metaphors of deception, battle, and destruction, which are compatible with a reading of cumulative deterioration. The study contributes by conceptualizing PPEC and illustrating the potential and the limits of LLM-assisted qualitative analysis in consumer research; it also offers managerial implications for emotionally responsive complaint management systems.

items.title: Post-traumatic headache as a window into persistent brain dysfunction after traumatic brain injury: an opinion article
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of death and disability worldwide, particularly among young adults and individuals of working age (1,2). Advances in prehospital care, neurosurgery, and intensive care have improved survival after TBI, increasing attention to the persistent symptoms and functional limitations that may affect long-term recovery and quality of life (1,2).Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is a secondary headache attributed to traumatic injury to the head, including TBI, and is among the most frequent neurological symptoms reported after TBI (3)(4)(5)(6). In this article, we specifically address PTH occurring in the context of TBI rather than the broader category of headache attributed to head injury without established TBI. Consistent with the International Classification of Headache Disorders, PTH that persists for more than three months is referred to here as persistent PTH (3). Persistent PTH may coexist with fatigue, cognitive complaints, sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, and limitations in daily activities (4)(5)(6), contributing to the complexity of long-term clinical recovery.Conventional measures of initial TBI severity, including the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), pupillary reactivity, and structural imaging findings, remain essential for acute assessment and prognosis.However, the relationship between the extent and characteristics of the initial injury and persistent symptoms is not straightforward, and individuals with apparently similar acute injury characteristics may follow different long-term recovery trajectories (4-6, 11, 12). This variability has increased interest in biological and functional processes that may persist or evolve after the acute injury (7)(8)(9).Against this background, we propose the hypothesis that persistent PTH may serve as a clinical window into persistent brain dysfunction after TBI. This concept does not imply that persistent PTH is itself a biomarker or that it demonstrates the presence of a specific underlying mechanism. Rather, we propose that its persistence may serve as a clinical signal warranting investigation of functional or biological abnormalities that are not fully characterized by conventional structural assessment. This hypothesis is considered across the TBI severity spectrum. However, the evidence discussed in this article derives from heterogeneous populations, including mild TBI and moderate-to-severe TBI, and findings from one severity group should not be assumed to generalize to another. Furthermore, evidence directly obtained from patients with persistent PTH remains more limited than evidence derived from broader TBI populations. Throughout this article, we therefore distinguish PTH-specific findings from mechanisms that remain biologically plausible on the basis of the broader TBI literature.Acute TBI severity remains a major determinant of early clinical outcomes. Measures such as the GCS, pupillary reactivity, and structural imaging findings are strongly associated with mortality and functional disability and remain fundamental for clinical decision-making and prognostic assessment (1,2,10). However, these measures were primarily developed to characterize the initial injury and estimate acute outcomes, and their ability to account for persistent symptoms and heterogeneous longterm recovery trajectories is more limited (11,12).Patients with apparently similar initial injury characteristics may experience markedly different longterm outcomes, including persistent headache, fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, emotional symptoms, and reduced quality of life (11,12). This variability suggests that the extent and characteristics of the initial injury alone do not fully capture the processes associated with long-term recovery.TBI initiates a cascade of biological events that may extend beyond the acute phase (7-9). Among these processes, neuroinflammation has been extensively investigated. Acute activation of microglia and astrocytes contributes to tissue responses following injury, whereas sustained or dysregulated inflammatory activity has been associated with blood-brain barrier alterations, persistent inflammatory signaling, and changes in neuronal function (7)(8)(9)(17)(18)(19). Importantly, evidence of persistent neuroinflammation after TBI derives predominantly from experimental studies and broader TBI populations and should not be interpreted as evidence that neuroinflammation directly causes persistent PTH. Rather, it provides a biologically plausible framework that requires specific validation in patients with persistent PTH.Altered nociceptive processing may represent another relevant mechanism. Central sensitization should be distinguished from nociplastic pain and other forms of altered nociceptive signaling because these concepts are related but not interchangeable (20,21). PTH-specific studies have identified sensory abnormalities, including cephalic allodynia, hyperalgesia, and altered pain modulatory responses, supporting abnormal nociceptive processing in at least a subset of patients with persistent PTH (22). Experimental evidence of hypersensitivity to calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) further supports the involvement of CGRP-related nociceptive pathways (23). However, these findings neither establish central sensitization as a universal mechanism nor demonstrate a single pathophysiological pathway underlying persistent PTH.A complementary perspective is provided by network neuroscience, which conceptualizes neurological dysfunction as potentially arising from disturbances in interactions among distributed brain networks rather than exclusively from focal structural damage (13)(14)(15). TBI studies have demonstrated persistent structural network abnormalities during recovery (24), while PTH-specific neuroimaging studies have identified alterations in resting-state functional connectivity involving pain-processing, painmodulatory, and affective networks (25,26). These findings provide more direct, although still limited, evidence that persistent PTH may be associated with alterations in brain network function.Persistent PTH also frequently co-occurs with fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, emotional symptoms, and reduced quality of life (4)(5)(6). Rather than representing different expressions of a single persistent biological condition, these manifestations may arise from partially overlapping, independent, or mutually reinforcing mechanisms. Their co-occurrence therefore underscores the heterogeneity of post-traumatic recovery and the need to investigate how different biological and functional processes contribute to individual symptom profiles.Within the framework proposed here, persistent PTH is considered a potential clinical window into persistent brain dysfunction rather than a validated biomarker, prognostic indicator, or surrogate measure of an underlying biological process. We use the term clinical window to describe an observable clinical feature whose persistence may signal the need to investigate ongoing functional or biological abnormalities that are not fully captured by conventional structural assessment. Thus, persistent PTH is proposed primarily as a clinical signal for further investigation, not as evidence that a specific pathophysiological process is present.We use the term persistent brain dysfunction as an umbrella concept encompassing ongoing abnormalities in neural function or biological processes after TBI, including altered nociceptive processing, disturbances in brain network function, and potentially persistent inflammatory activity. This definition does not imply a single mechanism, nor does it assume that these abnormalities are present in all individuals with persistent PTH or that persistent PTH is caused by any one of them.The distinction is important because the evidence supporting these potential mechanisms varies substantially. PTH-specific neuroimaging studies have demonstrated alterations in resting-state functional connectivity involving pain-processing and pain-modulatory networks, including periaqueductal gray-related connectivity, with some alterations associated with headache burden or the subsequent development of persistent PTH (25,26). By contrast, evidence for persistent neuroinflammation and several other chronic neurobiological abnormalities derives predominantly from broader TBI populations. These mechanisms should therefore be regarded as biologically plausible contributors requiring direct investigation in persistent PTH rather than as established pathophysiological correlates of the condition.Persistent PTH may also reflect greater overall symptom burden rather than a distinct biological state.Headache commonly co-occurs with sleep disturbance, fatigue, cognitive complaints, anxiety, depression, and other post-traumatic symptoms (4-6), and these factors may independently influence both headache persistence and measures of brain function. Pre-existing headache disorders, injury severity, medication use, cervical or extracranial pain generators, and psychological and behavioral factors may further contribute to clinical heterogeneity. Consequently, the presence or severity of persistent PTH cannot currently be assumed to indicate the presence, type, or magnitude of persistent brain dysfunction.Testing the proposed clinical-window hypothesis will therefore require prospective studies that combine detailed headache phenotyping with objective measures of brain function and biology while accounting for relevant confounding factors. Quantitative electroencephalography, neuroimagingderived connectivity measures, and molecular or inflammatory measures are candidate approaches that could be evaluated in this context (24,27,28,31). Artificial intelligence and machine-learning methods may complement these measures as analytical approaches for identifying multidimensional patterns or patient phenotypes, rather than representing biological or functional measures themselves (29,30).At present, none of these candidate approaches can be considered a validated biomarker of persistent PTH. Their value lies in testing whether persistent PTH is systematically associated with measurable patterns of post-traumatic dysfunction beyond headache severity and overall symptom burden.The hypothesis proposed in this article should be interpreted within several important limitations. First, evidence directly linking persistent PTH to measurable ongoing brain dysfunction remains limited.Although PTH-specific neuroimaging studies have identified alterations in functional connectivity (25,26), much of the evidence supporting persistent neuroinflammation, neurophysiological abnormalities, and other chronic biological processes derives from broader TBI populations. Extrapolation of these findings to persistent PTH therefore requires caution, and associations observed after TBI should not be assumed to represent mechanisms of persistent PTH.Second, persistent PTH is clinically and biologically heterogeneous. Headache phenotype, pre-existing headache disorders, TBI severity, sleep disturbance, fatigue, psychological symptoms, medication use, cervical or extracranial pain generators, and other post-traumatic symptoms may influence both headache persistence and measures of brain function. These factors provide alternative or complementary explanations for associations between persistent PTH and biological or functional abnormalities. Consequently, future studies should determine whether such associations remain after appropriate characterization and adjustment for relevant confounding factors.The proposed clinical-window hypothesis also generates testable predictions. If persistent PTH is associated with ongoing post-traumatic dysfunction beyond overall symptom burden, individuals with persistent PTH should demonstrate reproducible functional or biological abnormalities when compared with appropriately matched TBI survivors without persistent PTH. These associations should remain detectable after accounting for injury severity, pre-existing headache, headache phenotype, psychological symptoms, sleep disturbance, medication use, and other relevant clinical factors.Longitudinal studies should further determine whether changes in headache frequency, intensity, or disability are accompanied by changes in candidate neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or molecular measures.Conversely, failure to identify reproducible associations between persistent PTH and objective measures of post-traumatic dysfunction, particularly after controlling for symptom burden and relevant confounders, would argue against the proposed clinical-window hypothesis or restrict its applicability to specific patient subgroups. This possibility is important because the framework proposed here should be considered a testable hypothesis rather than an assumption that persistent headache necessarily reflects ongoing brain dysfunction.Future research should therefore prioritize prospective longitudinal designs with detailed headache phenotyping and appropriate comparison groups. Studies comparing TBI survivors with persistent PTH, TBI survivors without persistent PTH, and, where appropriate, individuals with primary headache disorders may help determine which findings are related specifically to persistent PTH, to TBI more broadly, or to chronic headache irrespective of trauma. Stratification by mild TBI and moderate-to-severe TBI will also be necessary because mechanisms and recovery trajectories may differ across injury severity.Multimodal studies integrating clinical phenotyping with neuroimaging, quantitative electroencephalography, and molecular measures may help determine whether reproducible patterns of dysfunction can be identified in specific persistent PTH subgroups. Artificial intelligence and machine-learning approaches may support the analysis of these multidimensional datasets and the identification of patient phenotypes, but their role is analytical and depends on the quality and validation of the underlying clinical and biological measures (24,(27)(28)(29)(30)(31). Candidate measures should not be considered biomarkers until their reproducibility, specificity, longitudinal behavior, and clinical relevance have been established in persistent PTH populations.Ultimately, the value of the proposed framework will depend on whether persistent PTH provides clinically meaningful information beyond established measures of injury severity and overall posttraumatic symptom burden. Prospective validation is therefore required before persistent PTH can be used to identify individuals for additional biological assessment, prognostic stratification, or mechanism-based interventions. Persistent PTH may provide a clinically accessible signal for investigating ongoing functional or biological abnormalities after TBI, but this relationship remains hypothetical and should not be interpreted as evidence that persistent headache is itself a biomarker of brain dysfunction.Distinguishing PTH-specific findings from abnormalities associated with TBI more broadly, controlling for alternative explanations and confounding factors, and prospectively testing the proposed associations will be essential to determine the validity and clinical relevance of this framework.

items.abstract: This study investigates the use of AI applications in film-based learning in upper secondary Spanish classes. It aims to explore learners’ processes, opportunities, and challenges when engaging with language, cultural, and analytical tasks supported by AI. Data were collected triangulatively through videographic classroom recordings, screen captures, and learners’ written products and analyzed using qualitative content analysis. Findings indicate that ChatGPT primarily supports learners in understanding content-related aspects and historical backgrounds, while active engagement with language, film aesthetics, and emotional perspectives remain limited. Learners recognize the limitations of AI-generated outputs and critically reflect on their incompleteness. The study contributes to the research field by empirically examining, for the first time, the intersection of filmbased learning, Spanish instruction, and AI use, providing implications for the didactic design of AI-supported film work.

items.title: Predicting Live Birth After Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF/ICSI: Differential ICM/Trophectoderm Morphology Encoding and a Hybrid Attention--Logistic Regression Ensemble
items.abstract: Predicting live birth before fresh embryo transfer could support shared decision-making in IVF/ICSI, but routine clinical data are small, heterogeneous, and contain pathway-dependent variables prone to outcome leakage. We aimed to construct a curated single-centre IVF/ICSI dataset and develop a prediction model suited to small tabular clinical data. \textit{Materials and Methods:} We assembled 616 fresh embryo-transfer cycles (251 live birth, 365 non-live birth) with clinical, laboratory, and embryological predictors, and embryo morphology encoded with a novel differential weighting of the inner cell mass and trophectoderm. After KNN imputation, robust scaling, and selection of 50 features, we developed a Hybrid Attention Network (HAN), a learnable feature-attention gate followed by a compact multilayer perceptron, and a HAN + logistic-regression (LR) ensemble with a validation-tuned weight. Models were benchmarked against classical machine learning, TabPFN, and text-serialized language models on a held-out test set; AUC-ROC was the primary metric. \textit{Results:} The HAN + LR ensemble achieved the highest test AUC-ROC (0.710; accuracy 0.710, F1 0.630), ahead of the HAN backbone alone (0.700), logistic regression (0.667), the TabPFN + LR hybrid (0.666), and TabPFN (0.650). Text-serialized language models performed near chance (AUC $\le$ 0.61). The differentially weighted trophectoderm feature ranked highest by consensus importance across models. \textit{Discussion:} A compact attention network combined with a linear model outperformed both components and strong foundation-model baselines on a small clinical cohort. \textit{Conclusion:} The curated dataset and HAN + LR ensemble offer a transparent, reproducible basis for IVF/ICSI live-birth prediction; external validation is the next step.

items.title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL ($D$) and error-step KL contrast ($Δd^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by $Δd^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$ also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.

items.title: Predictive performance of vital sign–based prediction models for in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Background In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is a major patient-safety event often preceded by detectable clinical deterioration. Vital sign–based cardiac arrest prediction models have been developed to identify hospitalized patients at increased risk of IHCA, but their predictive performance has not been quantitatively synthesized across studies. Methods This PRISMA-based systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO. Ovid Embase, Ovid MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) within the Cochrane Library were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating vital sign–based prediction models for IHCA in hospitalized general ward patients. Eligible models used routinely collected bedside vital signs as core predictors; models relying on laboratory values, imaging data, or other non-bedside-measured clinical variables as core predictors were excluded. The primary performance measure was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC); area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was extracted and summarized when reported. Risk of bias was assessed using PROBAST + AI (Prediction model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool + Artificial Intelligence). Results Of 10,645 records identified, six studies were included. The included studies evaluated Vital sign–based cardiac arrest prediction models, including Cardiac Arrest Risk Triage (CART), the deep learning–based early warning score (DEWS), and the deep learning–based cardiac arrest risk score (DeepCARS), and were published between 2012 and 2024. Three studies reported cardiac arrest-specific AUROC estimates suitable for the primary meta-analysis; the exploratory pooled AUROC was 0.89 (95% CI, 0.88–0.91; I² = 92%). Overall risk of bias was low in two studies, high in three, and unclear in one. Conclusions Vital sign–based cardiac arrest prediction models showed potentially useful discrimination for predicting IHCA; however, the pooled AUROC should be interpreted as an exploratory summary because only three studies contributed to the primary meta-analysis, heterogeneity was substantial, and half of all included studies were judged to have a high overall risk of bias. Standardized outcome definitions, external validation, and prospective evaluation of calibration, alert burden, and clinical utility are needed before broad clinical implementation.

items.title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
items.abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

items.title: PremiseSQL: Evaluating Premise Critique and Abstention in Text-to-SQL Systems
items.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have substantially improved Text-to-SQL performance, yet existing NL2SQL systems largely assume that user queries are valid and answerable. As a result, models often generate executable SQL even for queries with flawed premises. We introduce premise critique ability in NL2SQL, namely the ability to recognize flawed queries and abstain from generating misleading SQL. To evaluate this capability, we propose PremiseSQL, a benchmark containing 1,800 flawed NL2SQL queries across four categories of premise failures, along with their 1,800 original queries. We further design an evaluation framework to measure intrinsic and prompt-induced premise-aware behavior across three prompting settings. Experiments on frontier LLMs show that current models are strongly premise-trusting by default and rarely critique flawed premises. Stronger critique-oriented prompting improves detection and abstention on flawed queries, but also increases false invalid judgments and suppresses SQL generation on originals. The code is available at https://github.com/vegeet/PremiseSQL.

items.title: Preparing Teachers to Assess in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Integrative Review and Framework for Assessment-AI Knowledge
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, changes assessment by altering the evidential relationship among student work, learning, and professional judgment. Teachers must design tasks when students can readily obtain machine-generated responses, interpret automated feedback and analytics whose validity is conditional, and justify consequential decisions under uncertainty. This critical integrative review synthesizes scholarship on AI in education, assessment, teacher learning, and emerging professional-development interventions. It proposes Assessment-AI Knowledge (A-AIK) as an assessment-specific configuration of professional knowledge rather than a replacement for assessment literacy, AI literacy, or technological pedagogical content knowledge. A-AIK comprises three interdependent capacities: design competence, which establishes conditions for eliciting meaningful evidence; interpretive competence, which calibrates the meaning, uncertainty, and evidential weight of AI-mediated information; and justificatory competence, which supports transparent, fair, and reviewable decisions. Disciplinary authenticity, human agency, equity, transparency and data governance, and epistemic humility operate as cross-cutting commitments. The reviewed literature suggests that promising interventions use scenarios, authentic assessment redesign, structured critique, peer deliberation, and iterative classroom trials. Recurrent limitations include small samples, reliance on self-report, short duration, and measures of confidence or acceptance rather than demonstrated assessment performance. A four-phase professional-learning model—calibrate, redesign, enact, and justify, is proposed as a synthesis-informed design hypothesis requiring empirical evaluation. The article concludes with provisional performance indicators, institutional conditions, and a research agenda for responsible AI-mediated assessment.

items.abstract: Principles of Good Scientific Practice in Geoinformatics: From Data Management to Reproducible Code Trial lecture (Probevorlesung, § 13 HabilO) for the Venia Legendi in Geovisual Analytics at the Faculty of Environmental Sciences, Technische Universität Dresden (October 15, 2026, Dresden, Germany). Reflecting the core principles discussed, this lecture and its underlying pipeline are openly archived as a version-controlled, persistent resource to demonstrate reproducible scientific practice in action. Abstract Spatial data science occupies a uniquely vulnerable position in the ongoing reproducibility crisis. Below high-level Python libraries lies a complex stack of compiled C/C++ system libraries (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ) where unannounced datum shifts or compiler updates silently alter coordinates without throwing errors. Concurrently, spatial planning practice frequently relies on GUI-based desktop GIS workflows and binary office documents (`.docx`), leaving zero audit trail for legal scrutiny or scientific verification. Grounded in the normative framework of the DFG Code of Conduct (Guidelines 7, 10, 11, and 12) and Mayer's principles of multimedia learning, this lecture outlines four foundational pillars to transition from fragile ad-hoc scripts to resilient, verifiable scholarship: Part I • Diagnose (The Reality Check): Identifying the root failure modes of spatial data science—from the "spatial curse" of compiled system dependencies and unrecorded point-and-click operations to the administrative friction of managing 22,000+ data cells across municipal Word documents. Part II • Structure (The Resilient Archive): Establishing core architectural principles: Separation of Concerns (SoC), Single Source of Truth (SSOT), and Knowledge Longevity. Demonstrating that tools (Typora, QGIS, Zotero) are merely disposable viewing lenses, whereas disciplined plain text (Markdown) and open formats (GeoPackage, GeoParquet) constitute the permanent archive of thought. Addressing the FAIR vs. ELSA dilemma through synthetic twins and probabilistic hashing. Part III • Construct (Freezing the Computation): Demonstrating parameterized, headless GIS batch pipelines. Using an authentic planning case study (1,500 wind turbine viewsheds calculated via headless GRASS GIS inside JupyterLab for regional planning), the lecture illustrates literate provenance, isolated Docker container layering (Carto-Lab), and automated GitLab CI/CD release pipelines. Part IV • Evaluate (The Generative Frontier): Governing the integration of non-deterministic Large Language Models (LLMs). Establishing Prompts as Code and conversational lineage archiving to maintain human-in-the-loop accountability, separating probabilistic model outputs from verifiable scientific scholarship. The lecture concludes with a pragmatic survival checklist for Master's theses and frames Good Scientific Practice through the lens of Calm Technology: disciplined conventions do not add administrative burden - they liberate researchers from technical friction to focus on intellectual synthesis. items.title: Principles of occupational health: from peg legs to pension funds
items.abstract: Pirates, considered lawless barbarians, had a functioning and premium-free accident insurance system in the 17th century, the principles of which are also found in today's workers' compensation: collective risk-sharing, fixed compensation payments for injuries, and jointly financed benefits. Modern occupational health formalizes and significantly extends the pirates' rough-and-ready concept through legal and actuarial frameworks. For illustration, we compare the Pirate Codes or Articles with their compensation practice with today's occupational safety and health systems in the UK and Germany. Our comparison is confined to self-governing pirate communities.

items.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.abstract: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.

items.title: Producción virtual e infraestructura crítica : reconfiguración, acceso y sostenibilidad audiovisual
items.abstract: This article examines virtual production as a critical infrastructure of contemporary audiovisual practice, moving beyond its restricted understanding as a technical innovation or a set of tools designed to optimize shooting processes. The objective of the study is to analyze, through an integrative literature review, how specialized scholarship conceptualizes virtual production in relation to three strategic dimensions: the reconfiguration of the audiovisual pipeline, structural inequalities of access, and the conditions of sustainability and governance within the production ecosystem. Methodologically, a qualitative thematic review was conducted. From an initial pool of 68 records, selection criteria based on thematic relevance, conceptual density, and interpretative contribution were applied, resulting in a final corpus of 29 unique texts published between 2016 and 2026, including peer-reviewed articles, industry reports, doctoral theses, and technical documents. The analysis was structured around four interconnected axes: (1) virtual production as a sociotechnical system and critical infrastructure; (2) the transition from a linear production model toward iterative convergence and early integration across pre-production, production, and post-production; (3) unequal access, labor transformations, and professional training under the notion of “conditional democratization”; and (4) ecosystemic sustainability linked to technological governance, impact assessment, technical memory, and local capacity building. The findings indicate that virtual production not only transforms visual representation or the physical set but also reorganizes the material, informational, and institutional foundations of audiovisual labor. Furthermore, its expansion does not guarantee automatic democratization, as it depends on pre-existing infrastructures, specialized human capital, and stable collaborative frameworks. The study offers a critical and integrative reading of virtual production as a structural phenomenon shaping twenty-first-century audiovisual practice, particularly relevant to Latin America and Central America.

items.title: Professional identity as the missing link: Understanding motivational pathways among hotel employees
items.abstract: Hospitality research has often viewed motivation as the primary mechanism linking managerial practices to employee behavior. However, less attention has been paid to how employees interpret such practices before motivational responses emerge. Drawing on professional identity research, this study examines Professional Identity as an interpretive mechanism linking employees’ perceptions of Rewards and Transformational Leadership to Motivation and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Using survey data from 325 frontline hotel employees in South Korea, we test an individual-level model connecting Developmental Rewards, Material Rewards, Transformational Leadership, Professional Identity, Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, and OCB. The results show significant indirect associations between Developmental Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation and between Transformational Leadership and Intrinsic Motivation through Professional Identity. Developmental Rewards and Transformational Leadership were also indirectly associated with OCB through Professional Identity and Intrinsic Motivation. In contrast, the hypothesized Material Rewards pathways through Professional Identity and Extrinsic Motivation were not supported. These findings extend hospitality motivation research by highlighting the importance of identity-affirming managerial practices in frontline service settings.

items.title: Proposing an LLM-Based Framework for Automated Structuring and Verification of Korean Railway Software Safety Requirements
items.abstract: Railway signaling software must satisfy strict requirements—clarity, completeness, verifiability, and traceability—from the specification phase. KRS-SG-0069 requirements are written in Korean natural language, making manual structuring costly and expert-dependent. I propose a semi-automated framework combining LLM-based structuring with deterministic verification. Analysis of 94 requirements identified seven defect types mapped to EN 50128 clause 7.2.4 violations. The framework comprises four modules: M1 classifies requirements; M2 converts them into a six-element boilerplate via Chain-of-Thought prompting; M3 validates drafts through a four-layer rule engine; M4 generates state transition models, test cases, and a traceability matrix. The LLM is confined to draft generation, while safety judgments are delegated to deterministic engines and formal validators. This paper presents an architectural foundation; quantitative evaluation and broader applicability remain as future work.

items.title: Psychological Features of the Interrelation Between Occupational Stress and Emotional Burnout of Higher Education Teachers Under War Conditions
items.abstract: The paper offers a theoretical and analytical substantiation of the psychological features of the interrelation between occupational stress and emotional burnout of academic staff at Ukrainian higher education institutions working under the full-scale war. Several interrelated circumstances make the issue pressing. First, the work of a university teacher belongs to the "person-to-person" socionomic professions characterised by chronic emotional load, whereby prolonged exposure to stressors regularly develops into burnout. Second, war-related factors – a permanent threat to life, forced displacement, institutional relocation, distance and blended learning, power and communication disruptions – are superimposed on the "ordinary" academic stressors and greatly intensify them. Third, longitudinal observations reveal not an episodic but a progressive increase of burnout among Ukrainian teachers: the share of persons with a high level of emotional exhaustion rose from 49.5 % in July 2022 to 71.8 % in January 2024. Analysis of current scholarly sources – recent professional publications of 2023–2025, analytical reports and official statistics – made it possible to order the phenomenology of the "stress – burnout" link in the war context and to reveal the mechanism of transition from the former to the latter. The meanings of "occupational stress" and "emotional burnout syndrome" are clarified, the two are distinguished, and the genetic connection between them is shown. War stressors of a teacher are systematised into three groups – existential-security, organisational-professional, and communicative-emotional. A theoretical model of the stress–burnout interrelation is built, in which coping strategies, psychological resourcefulness and institutional support act as the key mediating links. A three-level system of burnout prevention – individual, group and institutional – is proposed together with a list of concrete measures. The materials obtained can be applied directly when designing programmes of psychological support for academic staff, planning measures to preserve their occupational health and making managerial decisions at the level of a higher education institution.

items.title: PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION MECHANISMS FOR ENSURING HIGHER EDUCATION QUALITY: RESULTS OF APPLICATION AND PROSPECTS FOR DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: The article examines the mechanisms of public administration for ensuring the quality of higher education in Ukraine through the prism of the classifications established in the scholarly discourse, as well as through the practices of their functioning and their actual impact on the international competitiveness of domestic higher education institutions. The methodological basis of the research combines the analysis of regulatory and legal acts, programme documents of the international and national levels, statistical data of the National Agency for Higher Education Quality Assurance, and a comparative analysis of the dynamics of the positioning of Ukrainian universities in the leading international rankings during 2022–2026. A contradiction has been identified between the architectonics of building the higher education quality assurance system and the comparatively low positioning of Ukrainian universities in international rankings (Quacquarelli Symonds World University Rankings; Times Higher Education World University Rankings; Academic Ranking of World Universities, ShanghaiRanking). In particular, it has been established that the number of Ukrainian universities represented in the QS World University Rankings decreased from 11 in 2023 to 4 in 2026, while the highest position of domestic institutions in the Times Higher Education ranking has consistently remained within the 801–1000 group despite the quantitative growth of their representation. The exhaustion of the potential of the traditional regulatory-legal, organisational- administrative and economic mechanisms of public administration in the higher education sphere has been substantiated, along with the need to search for new mechanisms of public administration for ensuring quality. The article also offers proposals on the necessity of applying innovative mechanisms for ensuring the quality of higher education, namely those grounded in the toolkit of artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and robotic process automation, the practical significance of which is confirmed by international experience and the analytical priorities of the national quality assurance system.

items.title: QUALITY OF HIGHER EDUCATION IN INDIA: CHALLENGES, OPPORTUNITIES AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
items.abstract: Higher education plays a pivotal role in shaping a nation's economic growth, technological advancement, and social development. India possesses one of the world's largest higher education systems, comprising over one thousand universities and thousands of colleges that collectively educate millions of students annually. Despite significant expansion in institutional capacity and enrolment over the past two decades, maintaining quality remains a major concern. Challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, faculty shortages, disparities in access, limited research productivity, employability gaps, insufficient industry-academia collaboration, governance issues, and unequal digital access continue to impede the realization of globally competitive higher education. Simultaneously, transformative initiatives including the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, digital learning platforms, research funding reforms, international collaborations, multidisciplinary education, and the integration of artificial intelligence present unprecedented opportunities for systemic improvement. This review critically examines the current status of higher education quality in India by synthesizing evidence from government reports, policy documents, and contemporary scholarly literature. The paper discusses the multidimensional challenges affecting educational quality and evaluates emerging opportunities driven by technological innovation, quality assurance mechanisms, competency-based curricula, and global academic partnerships. Furthermore, it proposes strategic recommendations to strengthen governance, faculty development, research ecosystems, institutional autonomy, accreditation, digital transformation, and employability. The study concludes that achieving sustainable excellence in higher education requires coordinated efforts among policymakers, regulatory agencies, academic institutions, industry, and society. A learner-centric, technology-enabled, research-oriented, and globally connected higher education system will be fundamental to realizing India's vision of becoming a global knowledge economy by 2047.

items.title: Quantitative Structure–Activity Relationships for Predicting Organic Contaminant Reactivity in Electrochemical Advanced Oxidation Processes: Descriptors, Kinetics, and Machine Learning Frontiers
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Electrochemical advanced oxidation processes (EAOPs) have become a prominent tool in wastewater remediation of refractory organic pollutants due to their versatility and ability to generate powerful, in situ oxidant species—predominantly hydroxyl radicals (•OH). Concurrently, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models have emerged as vital tools for predicting activity in high‐priority areas like drug development and toxicity. In this review, we address the application of QSARs in decoding reactivity within electrooxidation processes. We trace their evolution from early origins using the Hammett parameter () as a molecular descriptor to quantum chemical descriptors—such as , ionization potentials (IPs), and Fukui functions—and finally to advanced machine learning (ML) approaches like graph neural networks (GNNs) designed to navigate complex real wastewater matrices. Additionally, we highlight the anode as a core mechanistic variable that dictates oxidant selectivity. Finally, we discuss the primary limitations hindering ML adoption in EAOPs—including small training sets, a lack of electrochemical‐specific datasets, limited water‐matrix transferability, black‐box interpretability, and conflicting optimization metrics—and explore emerging strategies to overcome them, such as transfer learning, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and physics‐informed ML.

items.abstract: This volume examines one of the most important teacher–scholar projects of our time: innovating pedagogies and ethics in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). The volume brings together scholarship in three sections: Introductions, Digital Agency and Giving Students Voice, and Embodied Pedagogies. In this volume, we curate scholarship that engages with pedagogical governance for educators, digital storytelling, inclusive pedagogy, discussion boards, online student engagement, autoethnography, documentary-making, ecological consciousness, study practices, community-centered learning, and Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping. Taken together, this body of research demonstrates that meaningful learning is not only cognitive but also emotional, relational, and contextual, which requires pedagogies that attend to empathy, belonging, and lived experience. Across diverse contexts, educators are provided with pedagogical tools to support students in developing critical thinking and reflection skills while also fostering social responsibility and a commitment to the common good. All these elements are essential to this timely, interdisciplinary teacher–scholar project to support ethical AI in education.

items.title: RECENT ADVANCES IN ANALYTICAL CHEMISTRY: EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES, INNOVATIVE METHODOLOGIES AND SUSTAINABLE APPROACHES IN PHARMACEUTICAL ANALYSIS
items.abstract: Analytical chemistry plays an essential role in the identification, separation, quantification, and characterization of pharmaceutical substances. Recent technological developments have introduced advanced analytical approaches with improved sensitivity, accuracy, selectivity, speed, and reliability.[1] This review focuses on recent research in chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy, biosensors, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML), and Green Analytical Chemistry. Modern chromatographic and mass spectrometric techniques enable efficient separation, structural characterization, impurity profiling, and sensitive analysis of complex samples. Spectroscopic techniques provide rapid and non-destructive characterization, while biosensors offer sensitive, rapid, and potentially portable detection systems. AI/ML approaches are increasingly applied for analytical data processing, prediction, pattern recognition, and method optimization. Green analytical approaches aim to minimize hazardous solvents, waste generation, energy consumption, and sample requirements while maintaining analytical performance.[2] The review compares the methodologies, major findings, strengths, limitations, and research gaps reported in recent studies. Overall, the integration of advanced instrumentation, intelligent data analysis, biosensing technologies, and sustainable analytical practices is expected to contribute to the development of faster, more sensitive, reliable, automated, and environmentally sustainable pharmaceutical analytical methods.

items.title: Recent Trends in Caries Risk Assessment: A Critical Narrative Review of Predictive Validity, Artificial Intelligence, Biomarkers and Clinical Implementation
items.abstract: Caries risk assessment (CRA) is intended to estimate an individual's likelihood of developing new caries lesions or experiencing lesion progression over a defined period so that preventive, diagnostic and recall strategies can be tailored. Contemporary CRA is changing rapidly. Established approaches such as Cariogram, Caries Management by Risk Assessment (CAMBRA), professional checklists and risk-based care pathways are increasingly being supplemented by statistical prediction models, machine learning, digital self-assessment, salivary and microbiome biomarkers, and population-specific tools. This critical narrative review evaluates whether these developments have improved prognosis rather than merely increased technical complexity. Literature published principally from 2015 to 8 August 2026 was examined, while earlier seminal studies were retained when necessary to establish concepts and validation history. The synthesis distinguishes future-event prediction from cross-sectional detection or classification, because this distinction is frequently blurred in the recent literature. The strongest and most reproducible conventional predictor remains previous or current caries experience, while social conditions, fluoride exposure, plaque, diet, salivary function and life-course factors modify risk. Established multifactorial tools can structure clinical reasoning and risk-linked care, but external validation remains uneven and evidence that their use itself improves patient outcomes is limited. Machine-learning studies often report promising discrimination, yet many rely on cross-sectional outcomes, internal validation, small samples or incomplete calibration and clinical-utility assessment. Prospective cohorts demonstrate that simple, readily collected predictors can perform competitively, challenging assumptions that algorithmic complexity necessarily improves care. Salivary, microbiome and genetic approaches remain biologically informative but are not yet sufficiently standardised or externally validated for routine prognostic use. The most important recent trend is therefore methodological rather than technological: CRA is moving towards explicit prediction horizons, transparent validation, calibration, decision-linked utility, population transportability and repeated reassessment. Future progress will depend on prospective multicentre validation and impact studies that compare complex models against parsimonious clinical baselines and test whether risk-guided decisions improve outcomes without widening inequalities.

items.title: Reconfiguring the Production Value Chain
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping video production from a set of isolated tools into a core production infrastructure. This chapter presents an integrative value-chain framework showing how AI transforms pre-production, production, post-production, and distribution. It identifies four major shifts: workflow compression, creative augmentation, scale and personalization, and disintermediation. The chapter also examines the tension between democratization, in which low-cost AI tools empower small studios, educators, and creators in emerging economies, and consolidation, in which powerful firms control foundation models, compute, data, and distribution. Using cases on virtual production, AI-assisted localization, and the 2023 Hollywood labor agreements, it discusses key governance issues, including labor displacement, intellectual property disputes, content authenticity, and audience trust. It argues that AI is reorganizing video production as an economic system and offers recommendations for scholars, practitioners, and policymakers, especially in the Global South.

items.title: Recoverability-Controlled Safety Miscalibration in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Safety-aligned language models are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining useful for benign ones. However, because many evaluations score only the final response, they often conflate intent understanding with response-level safety behavior. To address this, we introduce RiskCueBench, a recoverability-controlled benchmark that separates these two stages by first measuring whether a model can successfully recover a high-level intent and then evaluating its safety behavior on the same prompt. RiskCueBench contains 160 latent intents and 640 abstract non-operational surface prompts across eight risk categories. The benchmark covers 25 completed model groups and 32,000 successful model outputs with final rubric-adjudicated labels. When conditioning on pairs where both surface forms are recoverable, we find that increased contextualized specificity induces a shift toward less safe behavior. Specifically, paired bootstrap estimates show that the refusal rate and global safety score decrease by 0.175 and 0.440, respectively. Furthermore, mixed effects modeling corroborates a 0.107 increase in unsafe cooperation. These results show that the safety behavior can be miscalibrated to the surface form even after the intent has been recovered, motivating safety evaluations that report response behavior conditional on semantic recoverability.

items.title: Reflections on Sociotechnical Change: New Directions for and Continuities in Research on New Technology, Work, and Employment
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This reflective article identifies three interconnected themes for advancing scholarship on new technology, work and employment. First, it calls for stronger theorisation of technology and deeper engagement with the political economy of Big Tech and AI. Attending to the material and political dimensions of technological systems is vital for challenging dominant narratives that present technologically driven change as inevitable. Second, the article argues for widening the empirical scope of research beyond the “new, new technologies,” while overlooking less visible sectors and the differing experiences of adopters and non‐adopters within the same industries. Broadening the empirical field and methodological repertoire would illuminate the uneven and variegated nature of digitalisation. Third, the article emphasises the importance of historical contextualisation. Situating contemporary developments within longer trajectories of workplace transformation is essential for understanding ongoing challenges and informing research on work futures.

items.title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

items.title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Measuring Harmful Reachability in Autoregressive Language Models
items.abstract: LLM safety evaluations via jailbreaking typically index on attack success rate (ASR): whether a generated response violates safeguards. However, ASR only evaluates sampled outputs and provides little information on the underlying generation process. Autoregressive language models define distributions over possible outputs, and a sampled refusal can coexist with substantial probability mass on harmful generation paths. We study this hidden structure through bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes and computes the finite-horizon probability that generation reaches a harmful continuation. BCA constructs a bounded continuation tree, labels terminal continuations with a semantic harm evaluator, and estimates harmful reachability using exact probabilistic model checking. BCA complements ASR by measuring how much harmful behavior remains accessible beneath a sampled safe response. This makes it useful for distinguishing models that look identical under measured ASR values, and allocating red-team effort toward regions of the generation process with greater hidden risk. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, we show that BCA effectively quantifies hidden harmful behavior and provides a useful signal to guide red teaming.

items.abstract: The worldwide demand for nutraceuticals and herbal products has grown rapidly due to their growing role in health promotion and disease prevention.Despite their widespread use, regulatory approaches differ substantially among countries, leading to inconsistencies in product quality, safety evaluation, and international commercialization.This review examines and compares the regulatory systems of the United States, the European Union, India, Japan, China, Canada, and Australia, with particular attention to product classification, marketing authorization, quality assurance, raw material standardisation, and post-market monitoring.Evidence from published reports was also assessed to identify the consequences of regulatory gaps.The analysis indicates that differences in regulatory expectations contribute to problems such as adulteration, contamination, incorrect botanical identification, and inconsistent product performance.Well-documented incidents, including Aristolochia-induced nephropathy, cardiovascular events linked to Ephedra-containing products, liver injury associated with Hydroxycut, and heavy metal contamination in certain Ayurvedic preparations, demonstrate the potential health risks arising from inadequate regulatory control.The findings emphasize the need for greater international alignment of regulatory practices, stronger standards for raw material quality, improved surveillance throughout the product lifecycle, and the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence to strengthen regulatory decision-making while accommodating country-specific regulatory frameworks.

items.title: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents
items.abstract: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.

items.title: Respiratory exposure to crystalline silica among ceramic industry workers in Iran: Exposure levels, deterministic risk assessment, Monte Carlo simulation, and spirometric indices
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The ceramic industry is an important component of Iran’s manufacturing sector; however, its complex production processes can generate respirable crystalline silica (RCS), a well-established occupational hazard associated with adverse respiratory outcomes. Objectives This study aimed to characterize RCS exposure levels, assess associated occupational health risks, and evaluate pulmonary function among ceramic workers in Iran. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among ceramic workers using a Similar Exposure Group (SEG) approach. A total of 79 personal respirable dust samples were collected across seven production tasks. RCS concentrations were determined according to NIOSH Method 7601 using a JENWAY 6105 UV/Visible spectrophotometer. Deterministic health risk assessment and Monte Carlo simulation (1,000 iterations) were performed based on the U.S. EPA methodology. Pulmonary function was assessed using spirometry, including forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV 1 ), forced vital capacity (FVC), and the FEV 1 /FVC ratio. Associations between RCS exposure and pulmonary function parameters were evaluated statistically. Results Mean RCS concentrations varied substantially across production tasks, ranging from 0.02 mg/m 3 in glazing operations to 0.50 mg/m 3 in crushing operations. Exposure levels among crusher workers and ball-mill spray operators significantly exceeded the occupational exposure limit of 0.025 mg/m 3 (p < 0.05). Deterministic risk assessment yielded hazard quotient (HQ) values below 1; however, Monte Carlo simulation showed that the 95th percentile HQ slightly exceeded 1, indicating an increased non-carcinogenic risk under high-exposure scenarios. Spirometric results were predominantly within normal ranges, although borderline obstructive and restrictive patterns were observed among packing and furnace workers. Significant negative correlations were observed between RCS concentration and FEV 1 (r s = −0.77, p = 0.04) and the FEV 1 /FVC ratio (r s = −0.78, p = 0.03). Conclusions Ceramic workers, particularly those involved in crushing and ball-mill operations, may experience substantial RCS exposure and increased respiratory health risks. The observed associations between RCS exposure and reduced pulmonary function highlight the need for effective engineering controls, respiratory protection programs, routine exposure monitoring, and periodic medical surveillance to reduce occupational health risks in the ceramic industry.

items.title: Responsible AI Governance as an Organisational Capability: A Theory-Building Integrative Review for Sustainable Organisations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organisational decision-making, creating opportunities for innovation and sustainability while intensifying concerns about accountability, transparency, stakeholder responsibility and human oversight. This structured theory-building integrative review synthesises a purposively bounded corpus of 35 unique works on responsible AI, AI governance, responsible leadership and organisational sustainability. Responsible AI Governance (RAIG) is conceptualised as a multidimensional organisational capability: the repeatable, coordinated and adaptive capacity through which responsible AI principles are translated into governance structures, decision processes, accountability arrangements, stakeholder relationships, human oversight and assurance across the AI lifecycle. Six interdependent dimensions are specified: ethical-strategic alignment, accountability architecture, human oversight and agency, stakeholder inclusion, transparency and assurance and lifecycle governance and adaptability. Responsible leadership is positioned as an antecedent managerial microfoundation rather than a constitutive dimension of RAIG. The framework separates sustainability from the content of RAIG and theorises sustainable organisational and stakeholder outcomes as consequences of effective governance. Propositions and a staged research programme establish a foundation for construct operationalisation, cross-context validation and subsequent nomological testing.

items.title: Responsible AI in Digital Marketing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence now shapes digital marketing, influencing targeting, personalization, pricing, content creation, and customer engagement. However, its use creates risks including algorithmic bias, personalization–privacy tensions, manipulative interface design, and declining consumer trust following AI disclosure. This chapter addresses a gap by integrating these risks with the design and governance mechanisms needed for responsible AI in digital marketing. Drawing on research in marketing, information systems, public administration, and law, it examines algorithmic risk, consumer trust, explainability, transparency, governance, and regulation. The review identifies consumer trust as the key mechanism linking algorithmic risk to marketing outcomes and proposes an integrated framework in which fairness auditing, consent-based data practices, responsible interface design, and explainability act as design levers, while governance and regulation establish implementation conditions. The chapter argues that responsible AI can help manage algorithmic risk and build trust.

items.title: Responsible AI Practices in Digital Marketing for MSMEs
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming digital marketing by enabling automation and personalization. For micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), AI offers opportunities to enhance competitiveness despite limited resources. However, adoption introduces risks such as privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, and cybersecurity threats that may undermine customer trust. These challenges are especially critical in emerging economies facing financial and technical constraints. The primary objective of this chapter is to systematically investigate the intersection of AI and digital marketing strategies among MSMEs in Oman, aligning responsible practices with Oman Vision 2040. Employing a qualitative, conceptual desk research methodology built on a systematic literature review, this study applies Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE), Trust, and Stakeholder frameworks to identify operational barriers and propose a sustainable growth framework centered on transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy, and human oversight.

items.abstract: As generative AI tools rapidly integrate into higher education—assisting with instruction, content generation, student evaluation, and research—universities face a complex landscape of ethical challenges.
