items.title: Responsible integration of generative AI and LLMs in higher education: Empirical insights and a framework for teaching and learning
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are rapidly reshaping university learning environments, yet pedagogical and ethical frameworks have not developed at the same pace as their adoption. Adopting a multidisciplinary approach, this study combines empirical evidence from a survey of 117 undergraduate Engineering and Health Sciences students with the pedagogical perspectives of university lecturers. It examines how students currently use GenAI and how these tools can be meaningfully integrated into teaching and learning. Findings show that students’ first exposure to GenAI is mainly driven by informal social media channels rather than institutional guidance, resulting in uneven and often unguided adoption. The study also identifies a “contradictory profile” in 11% of the sample: students who perceive GenAI use as a form of cheating while also expressing a strong demand for formal training on its academic integration. From the lecturers’ perspective, GenAI offers opportunities to support content creation, assessment design, and instructional workflows, provided that human-led teaching remains central. By integrating observed student behaviors with expert recommendations, this research proposes an ethical framework and practical guidelines for the responsible integration of GenAI in higher education. The study highlights the urgent need for institutional policies that address emerging socio-ethical tensions and ensure that GenAI enhances, rather than circumvents, foundational knowledge, academic integrity, and critical thinking.

items.title: Rethinking AI integration in African higher education: a mixed-methods investigation of capacity, equity, and governance across sub-Saharan Africa
items.abstract: The Revolutionizing Tertiary Education for Africa's Thriving AI Economy and Workforce (RetAIn) project presents a comprehensive, multi-method investigation into the conditions, constraints, and catalysts shaping Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption across African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Deploying both qualitative multi-stakeholders Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) from three African countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia) and a quantitative cross-country survey across five Sub-Saharan African nations (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia, Kenya, and Zambia), this study produces a richly triangulated account of AI integration dynamics on the continent. The FGD strand revealed a stark divergence in national AI trajectories: Rwanda operates under a strong top-down policy vision hindered by institutional rigidity; Namibia exhibits pragmatic institutional adaptability constrained by geographic and economic smallness; and Ghana demonstrates emergent, bottom-up innovation within a national policy vacuum. The survey strand, drawing on 156 responses across five countries, corroborated these qualitative tensions, documenting widespread recognition of AI's strategic importance alongside limited structured engagement, persistent infrastructure deficits, and marked equity barriers, particularly for women, vulnerable groups, rural students, and part-time workers. From both methods, a unifying finding emerges: AI integration in African HEIs consistently fails when technical adoption outpaces social, pedagogical, and governance co-evolution. The study argues for context-specific, socio-technically grounded strategies that pair curriculum co-design with robust industry partnerships, that centre equity and cultural relevance, and build governance frameworks capable of guiding, rather than chasing, technological change.

items.title: RETHINKING TRANSLATOR TRAINING AS A CROSS-CUTTING TECHNOLOGICAL WORKFLOW
items.abstract: Modern translator training faces a structural mismatch: technology is typically taught as a set of isolated modules, one tool per topic, while professional translation practice treats these same tools as an interconnected workflow in which a single instrument routinely performs functions attributed to several distinct stages. This article reframes the transla- tion process as a technological chain comprising four interrelated components – pre-translation analysis, CAT-assisted translation supported by an AI agent, quality management, and file preparation – and argues that these components are better represented as a network of overlapping actions than as a linear sequence of self-contained stages. Drawing on both theoretical models of translator competence (PACTE’s instrumental competence, the EMT framework) and empirical studies of specific tools and stages, the article identifies a gap between well-established theoretical support for cross- cutting technical competence and its still-fragmented empirical and classroom validation. The study demonstrates, through classroom examples – including the pre-editing of auto-generated video subtitles using regular expressions and a compar- ative analysis of PDF-document translation across several CAT environments – that a single technological action routinely crosses the boundaries between the four proposed stages, undermining the pedagogical logic of modular instruction. The article proposes a network model of the translation technological chain, in which the four components function as condi- tional nodes connected by feedback and cross-cutting links rather than fixed sequential order, and grounds this model in the broader concept of a translator’s digital literacy. The findings support a concrete pedagogical principle: technical com- petence formation should be organized around cross-cutting, project-based assignments that require students to move across several nodes of the model, rather than around isolated tool-specific modules. The article concludes by identifying directions for further research, including the applicability of the proposed model to team-based translation workflows and an unresolved gap between the documented professional importance of quality-management tools and students’ compar- atively modest perception of their value.

items.title: ReviewPilot: A Multi-Agent System for Screening and Data Extraction in Systematic Reviews
items.abstract: Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. We develop a conversational multi-agent system called ReviewPilot that automates the PRISMA workflow from paper screening to information extraction. Researchers can tailor criteria and schemas through dialogue, and a project memory keeps their configurations and revisions. Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source. On epidemiological expert reviews, ReviewPilot outperforms a single-prompt LLM and AgentSLR across three LLMs, with screening macro F1 up to 0.776 and extraction F1 up to 0.788. Case studies in biomedicine and human-computer interaction show close agreement with human annotators, suggesting that ReviewPilot can transfer beyond epidemiology. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/ReviewPilot.

items.title: Risk and Refusal: Mechanisms of LLM Responses to Suicidal Ideation
items.abstract: Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.

items.title: Role of Influencer Marketing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence to Build Consumer Trust in Brands
items.abstract: This chapter aims to explore the intricate relationship between authenticity, trust, and consumer loyalty in influencer marketing. Authenticity is pivotal in influencer marketing, where consumers, inundated with curated content, crave honesty and relatable experiences. Genuine passion from influencers for brands builds trust and transparency, connecting brands with consumers. This connection fosters positive brand perceptions and purchase intent.. By demystifying the role of authenticity in influencer marketing, this chapter aims to empower brands to circumnavigate the digital landscape effectively and build genuine relationships with their target audiences. Ultimately, it pursues to underwrite to a more transparent and trustworthy influencer marketing environment that benefits both consumers and brands. However, the advent of AI Technology and the rapid progress in this field have helped marketers to identify these challenges and solve their inherent problems. Also, AI today truly provides new and exciting avenues for marketing companies.
